verses.text: These are the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah. In the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, I was at the palace in Susa.
Hanani, one of my brothers, came with some men from Judah. I asked them about the Jews who’d escaped and survived the exile, and I asked how Jerusalem was doing.
They told me, “The people who survived the exile and are still there in the province are in deep trouble and are being shamed. Jerusalem’s wall is broken down, and its gates have been burned.”
When I heard that, I sat down and cried. I mourned for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven.
I said, “Please, LORD, God of heaven, great and awesome God, you keep your covenant and show faithful love to those who love you and keep your commands.

Please listen closely and keep your eyes open to hear your servant’s prayer. I’m praying before you day and night for your servants, the Israelites, and confessing the sins we’ve committed against you. I’ve sinned too, and so has my family.
We’ve done terribly wrong against you. We haven’t kept the commands, statutes, or rulings you gave your servant Moses.
“Please remember what you told Moses your servant: ‘If you do wrong, I’ll scatter you among the peoples.

But if you come back to me, keep my commands, and live by them, even if your scattered people are at the farthest edge of the sky, I’ll gather them from there. I’ll bring them to the place I’ve chosen for my name to dwell.’
“These are your servants, your own people. You rescued them by your great power and your strong hand.

Lord, please listen to your servant’s prayer and to the prayers of your servants who gladly honor your name with reverence. Help your servant succeed today and let this man show him mercy.” I was the king’s cupbearer.
In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, the wine was set out in front of him. I picked it up and served him. I’d never looked sad in front of him before.
The king asked me, “Why do you look so sad? You’re not sick. You’ve got to be hurting inside.” I was terrified.
I said to the king, “May the king live forever! Why wouldn’t I look sad? The city where my ancestors are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned down.”
Then the king asked, “What are you asking for?” So I prayed to the God of heaven.
I said, “If it pleases the king and I’ve found favor with you, please send me to Judah, to the city where my ancestors are buried, so I can rebuild it.”
The queen was sitting beside him when the king asked me, “How long will you be gone? When will you come back?” The king agreed to send me, and I gave him a time.
I also said, “If it pleases the king, please give me letters for the governors beyond the River so they’ll let me pass through until I reach Judah.

And please give me a letter for Asaph, who looks after the king’s forest, so he’ll give me timber for the gates of the fortress by the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I’ll live in.” The king gave me what I asked for because my God’s good hand was on me.
I went to the governors beyond the River and gave them the king’s letters. The king had sent army officers and horsemen with me.
When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard about it, they were deeply upset that someone had come to look out for the Israelites.
So I reached Jerusalem and stayed there for three days.
Then I got up in the night with a few men. I hadn’t told anyone what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem. The only animal with me was the one I was riding.
That night I went out through the Valley Gate, toward the Jackal’s Well and on to the Dung Gate. I checked Jerusalem’s walls and saw they were broken down and its gates had burned.
Then I went on to the Spring Gate and the King’s Pool, but there wasn’t enough room for the animal I was riding to get through.
So I went up along the stream in the dark and looked over the wall. Then I turned around and came back in through the Valley Gate.
The officials had no idea where I’d gone or what I’d done. I hadn’t told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, or anyone else who would do the work.

Then I said to them, “You can see what a mess we’re in. Jerusalem is in ruins, and its gates have been burned down. Come on, let’s rebuild Jerusalem’s wall so we don’t have to live with this disgrace.”
I told them how my God’s good hand had been on me and what the king had said to me. They answered, “Let’s get up and build!” So they got ready to do the good work.

When Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and Geshem the Arabian heard about it, they mocked us and treated us with contempt. “What do you think you’re doing?” they said. “Are you rebelling against the king?”
I answered, “The God of heaven will make our work succeed. We’re his servants, and we’re going to get up and build. You have no share, no right, and no remembrance in Jerusalem.”

Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests got up and built the Sheep Gate. They set it apart as holy and hung its doors. They also set apart the stretch as far as the Tower of Hammeah and the Tower of Hananel.
The men of Jericho built next to him, and Zaccur son of Imri built next to them.
Hassenaah’s sons built the Fish Gate. They laid its beams and fitted its doors, bolts, and bars.
Next to them, Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, made repairs. Next to him, Meshullam son of Berechiah, son of Meshezabel, made repairs, and Zadok son of Baana worked next to him.
The men of Tekoa worked next to them, but their nobles wouldn’t shoulder the Lord’s work.
Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah repaired the Old Gate. They laid its beams and fitted its doors, bolts, and bars.
Next to them, Melatiah the Gibeonite, Jadon the Meronothite, and the men of Gibeon and Mizpah repaired the residence of the governor beyond the River.
Next to him, Uzziel son of Harhaiah and the goldsmiths made repairs. Hananiah, one of the perfumers, worked next to him. They fortified Jerusalem as far as the Wide Wall.
Next to them worked Rephaiah son of Hur, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem.
Jedaiah son of Harumaph worked next to them, across from his house, and Hattush son of Hashabneiah worked next to him.
Malchijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahathmoab repaired another stretch and the Tower of the Furnaces.
Next to him, Shallum son of Hallohesh, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, worked on the repairs with his daughters.
Hanun and the people of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate. They rebuilt it, put in its doors, bolts, and bars, and repaired a thousand cubits of wall as far as the Dung Gate.
Malchijah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth Haccherem, rebuilt the Dung Gate and put in its doors, bolts, and bars.

Shallun son of Colhozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, rebuilt the Spring Gate. He covered it and fitted its doors, bolts, and bars. He repaired the wall by the Pool of Shelah next to the king’s garden, all the way to the stairs down from David’s city.
After him, Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth Zur, worked as far as the place across from David’s tombs, the man-made pool, and the House of the Mighty Men.
After him the Levites worked on the repairs. Rehum son of Bani worked there, and next to him Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, made repairs for his district.
After him their fellow Levites made repairs, including Bavvai son of Henadad, ruler of half the district of Keilah.
Next to him, Ezer son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another stretch across from the way up to the armory where the wall turns.
After him, Baruch son of Zabbai worked hard on another stretch, from the turn in the wall to the door of Eliashib the high priest’s house.
After him, Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, repaired another stretch from Eliashib’s front door to the end of his house.
After him, the priests from the surrounding area made repairs.
After them, Benjamin and Hasshub worked across from their house. After them, Azariah son of Maaseiah, son of Ananiah, made repairs beside his own house.
After him, Binnui son of Henadad repaired another stretch from Azariah’s house to the turn in the wall and on to the corner.
Palal son of Uzai worked across from the turn in the wall and the tower that sticks out from the upper royal house beside the guard court. Pedaiah son of Parosh worked after him.
The temple servants lived on Ophel, as far as the place opposite the Water Gate to the east and the tower that sticks out.
After him, the men of Tekoa repaired another stretch across from the big tower that sticks out, as far as the wall of Ophel.
Above the Horse Gate, the priests made repairs, each working across from his own house.
After them, Zadok son of Immer worked across from his own house, and Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, who guarded the East Gate, worked after him.
After him, Hananiah son of Shelemiah and Hanun, Zalaph’s sixth son, repaired another stretch. After them, Meshullam son of Berechiah worked across from his room.

After him, Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths, repaired the stretch up to the house of the temple servants and merchants. It was across from the Hammiphkad Gate and reached the uphill path at the corner.
The goldsmiths and merchants repaired the stretch from the uphill path at the corner to the Sheep Gate.
When Sanballat heard we were building the wall, he got furious and started mocking the Jews.

He said in front of his brothers and Samaria’s army, “What are these weak Jews doing? Are they going to fortify the place? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they finish in a day? Are they going to bring those burned stones back to life from piles of rubble?”
Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him. He said, “That stone wall they’re building? A fox could climb up and bring it down.”
“Listen, our God. They’re treating us with contempt. Turn their insults back on their own heads. Hand them over as plunder in a land where they’ll be captives.
Don’t cover up their wrongdoing or erase their sin from your sight. They’ve insulted the builders.”
So we kept building. The whole wall was joined up to half its height because the people were ready to work.
But Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites got furious when they heard that repairs on Jerusalem’s walls were moving ahead and that the gaps were closing.
They all plotted together to fight against Jerusalem and throw us into confusion.
But we prayed to our God and posted guards against them day and night.
The people of Judah said, “The people carrying the loads are running out of strength. There’s so much rubble that we can’t build the wall.”
Our enemies said, “They won’t know or see a thing until we’re right there among them, killing them and shutting down the work.”
When the Jews who lived near them came, they told us ten times from every direction, “Wherever you turn, they’ll attack us.”
So I posted guards in the low spots behind the wall, in the open areas. I stationed the people by families with their swords, spears, and bows.

I looked things over, stood up, and told the nobles, the officials, and everyone else, “Don’t be afraid of them! Remember the Lord, great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, sons, daughters, wives, and homes.”
When our enemies heard we knew about their plot and that God had wrecked their plans, we all went back to the wall, each to our own work.
From then on, half my servants did the work and half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of armor. The officials stood behind all the people of Judah.
The wall builders and the people carrying loads took up their work. Each person worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other.
Each builder wore his sword at his side while he worked. The man who blew the trumpet stayed beside me.
I told the nobles, the officials, and everyone else, “This is a big job spread over a long stretch. We’re far apart along the wall.
Wherever you hear the trumpet, gather with us there. Our God will fight for us.”
So we worked, and half the people held spears from daybreak until the stars came out.
At the same time I told the people, “Everyone should stay inside Jerusalem with their servants. That way they can stand guard for us at night and work during the day.”
So none of us took off our clothes, not me, my brothers, my servants, or the guards who followed me. Everyone took his weapon even when he went for water.
Then the people and their wives raised a loud outcry against their fellow Jews.
Some said, “There are a lot of us, with all our sons and daughters. We need grain so we can eat and stay alive.”
Others said, “We’re putting up our fields, vineyards, and houses as security just to get grain in this famine.”
Still others said, “We’ve borrowed money to pay the king’s tax, putting up our fields and vineyards as collateral.

We’re flesh and blood just like our fellow Jews, and our children are just like theirs. Yet we’re having to send our sons and daughters into slavery. Some of our daughters are already enslaved, and there’s nothing we can do about it. Other people have our fields and vineyards.”
When I heard their outcry and what they were saying, I got really angry.
I thought it over, then confronted the nobles and officials. I said, “You’re charging interest to your own people!” I called a big assembly to bring the charges against them.

I told them, “As far as we could, we bought back our fellow Jews who’d been sold to other nations. Now you’re selling your own people, so we have to buy them back from you?” They went quiet and couldn’t find a word to say.
I went on, “What you’re doing is wrong. Shouldn’t you live in reverence for our God and keep our enemies, the other nations, from mocking us?
My brothers, my servants, and I are lending them money and grain too. Please, let’s stop charging this interest.
Give them back their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses today. Give back the hundredth part of the money, grain, new wine, and oil you’ve been charging them.”
They said, “We’ll give it all back and demand nothing from them. We’ll do exactly what you say.” So I called the priests and made the nobles and officials swear to keep their promise.

I also shook out the fold of my robe and said, “May God shake anyone who breaks this promise out of their home and away from everything they’ve worked for. May they be shaken out and left empty like this.” The whole assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the LORD. The people kept their promise.
From the time I was appointed governor in Judah, from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes, twelve years in all, my brothers and I didn’t take the governor’s food allowance.

The governors before me lived at the people’s expense. They took bread and wine from them, plus forty shekels of silver. Even their servants bossed the people around. I didn’t do that because I feared God.
I stuck with the work on this wall. We didn’t buy any land, and all my servants gathered there to work.
I had 150 Jewish men and officials at my table, besides those who came to us from the nations around us.

Every day one ox, six choice sheep, and some birds were prepared for me. Every ten days there was a fresh supply of all kinds of wine. Even with all that, I didn’t demand the governor’s allowance because the burden on these people was already heavy.
Remember me, my God, for all the good I’ve done for these people.
Word got to Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arabian, and the rest of our enemies that I’d rebuilt the wall and closed every gap. At that point I still hadn’t hung the doors in the gates.
Sanballat and Geshem sent me a message: “Come meet us in the villages on the plain of Ono.” But they meant to hurt me.
I sent messengers back to tell them, “I’m doing important work here, so I can’t come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to come down to you?”
They sent me the same message four times. Each time I gave them the same answer.
The fifth time, Sanballat sent his servant to me the same way, this time with an open letter in his hand.

It said, “Word’s going around among the nations, and Gashmu says it too, that you and the Jews are planning to rebel. That’s why you’re building the wall, and from what people are saying, you plan to be their king.
You’ve even appointed prophets to announce in Jerusalem, ‘There’s a king in Judah!’ The king is going to hear all this. So come on, let’s talk it over.”
I sent him this reply: “None of what you’re saying is happening. You made it all up in your own head.”
They were all trying to scare us, thinking, “They’ll lose their nerve and never finish the job.” But now, strengthen my hands.

I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was shut in at home. He said, “Let’s meet inside the temple, in God’s house, and close the temple doors. They’re coming to kill you. Yes, they’re coming to kill you tonight.”
I said, “Should someone like me run away? Who in my position would go into the temple to save his own life? I’m not going in.”
I realized God hadn’t sent him. He’d spoken that prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.
They’d paid him to scare me into doing it and sinning. Then they could spread a bad report about me and shame me.
“My God, remember what Tobiah and Sanballat did. Remember Noadiah the prophet and the rest of the prophets who tried to scare me.”
So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days.
When all our enemies heard, the nations around us were afraid and lost their confidence. They realized our God had done this work.
In those days the nobles of Judah kept sending letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah kept writing back to them.
Many people in Judah were bound to him by oath because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah. His son Jehohanan had also married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah.
They told me about Tobiah’s good deeds and then reported what I said back to him. Tobiah sent letters to scare me.
Once the wall was built, I hung the doors, and the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites were appointed.
I put my brother Hanani and Hananiah, the commander of the fortress, in charge of Jerusalem. Hananiah was trustworthy and feared God more than most people did.

I told them, “Keep Jerusalem’s gates closed until the sun gets hot. Have the gatekeepers shut the doors while they’re still on duty, and bar them. Assign people from Jerusalem to guard shifts, each at their post and near their own home.”
The city was large and spread out, but few people lived in it, and the houses hadn’t been built.
My God put it in my heart to gather the nobles, officials, and people to register them by family. I found the family records of the first people who’d come back. Here’s what was written there:
These are the people of the province who came home from exile. King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had taken them away, and they returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to their own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, and Baanah. Here’s the count of the men of Israel:
Parosh’s descendants: 2,172.
Shephatiah’s descendants: 372.
Arah’s descendants: 652.
Pahathmoab’s descendants, from the lines of Jeshua and Joab: 2,818.
Elam’s descendants: 1,254.
Zattu’s descendants: 845.
Zaccai’s descendants: 760.
Binnui’s descendants: 648.
Bebai’s descendants: 628.
Azgad’s descendants: 2,322.
Adonikam’s descendants: 667.
Bigvai’s descendants: 2,067.
Adin’s descendants: 655.
Ater’s descendants from Hezekiah’s line: 98.
Hashum’s descendants: 328.
Bezai’s descendants: 324.
Hariph’s descendants: 112.
People from Gibeon: 95.
Men from Bethlehem and Netophah: 188.
Men from Anathoth: 128.
Men from Beth Azmaveth: 42.
Men from Kiriath Jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth: 743.
Men from Ramah and Geba: 621.
Men from Michmas: 122.
Men from Bethel and Ai: 123.
Men from the other Nebo: 52.
The other Elam’s descendants: 1,254.
Harim’s descendants: 320.
People from Jericho: 345.
People from Lod, Hadid, and Ono: 721.
People from Senaah: 3,930.
Here are the priests: Jedaiah’s descendants from Jeshua’s family: 973.
Immer’s descendants: 1,052.
Pashhur’s descendants: 1,247.
Harim’s descendants: 1,017.
The Levites were the descendants of Jeshua, Kadmiel, and the line of Hodevah: 74.
The singers were Asaph’s descendants: 148.
The gatekeepers came from the families of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai: 138 in all.
The temple servants came from these families: Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth,
Keros, Sia, Padon,
Lebana, Hagaba, Salmai,
Hanan, Giddel, Gahar,
Reaiah, Rezin, Nekoda,
Gazzam, Uzza, Paseah,
Besai, Meunim, Nephushesim,
Bakbuk, Hakupha, Harhur,
Bazlith, Mehida, Harsha,
Barkos, Sisera, Temah,
Neziah, and Hatipha.
The descendants of Solomon’s servants came from these families: Sotai, Sophereth, Perida,
Jaala, Darkon, Giddel,
Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth Hazzebaim, and Amon.
Altogether there were 392 temple servants and descendants of Solomon’s servants.
These people came up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer. They couldn’t show from their family records or ancestry whether they belonged to Israel:
The descendants of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda: 642.
From the priestly families there were descendants of Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai. Barzillai had married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and taken their family name.
They searched for their family records but couldn’t find them. So they were ruled ineligible and removed from the priesthood.
The governor told them they couldn’t eat any of the most holy things until a priest could serve with the Urim and Thummim.
The whole assembly totaled 42,360,
plus 7,337 male and female servants. They had 245 singers, men and women.
They had 736 horses and 245 mules,
435 camels and 6,720 donkeys.
Some of the family heads gave to the work. The governor gave the treasury 1,000 gold darics, 50 basins, and 530 sets of priests’ clothes.
Some family heads gave the treasury for the work 20,000 gold darics and 2,200 silver minas.
The rest of the people gave 20,000 gold darics, 2,000 silver minas, and 67 sets of priests’ clothes.
The priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, some of the people, and the temple servants settled in their towns, and so did all Israel. By the seventh month, the Israelites were in their towns.
All the people came together as one in the square in front of the Water Gate. They asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of the law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded Israel to follow.
On the first day of the seventh month, Ezra the priest brought the law before the whole assembly, men, women, and everyone old enough to understand what they heard.

There in front of the square at the Water Gate, he read from early morning until noon before the men, women, and everyone who could understand. The people paid close attention as he read the book of the law.

Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform they’d built for the occasion. Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah stood to his right. Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam stood to his left.
Ezra opened the book where everyone could see him, since he was standing above the crowd. As soon as he opened it, everyone stood up.
Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God. The whole crowd raised their hands and answered, “Amen, amen!” Then they bowed their heads and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.

Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites helped the people understand the law while everyone stayed where they were.
They read clearly from the book of God’s law and explained what it meant so the people could understand what they were hearing.

Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who taught the people told everyone, “Today is holy to the LORD your God. Don’t mourn or cry.” The people had all started crying when they heard the words of the law.
Then he told them, “Go, eat rich food and drink something sweet. Send some to anyone who has nothing ready. Today is holy to our Lord. Don’t be sad, because the joy of the LORD is your strength.”
The Levites calmed everyone down. “Quiet now,” they said. “This day is holy. Don’t be sad.”
The people went off to eat, drink, share their food, and celebrate because they understood the words they’d been told.
On the second day, the family heads of all the people came together with the priests and Levites around Ezra the scribe to study what the law said.
They found it written in the law that the LORD had commanded through Moses that the Israelites should live in shelters during the festival in the seventh month.

They were to spread the word in all their towns and in Jerusalem: “Go out to the hills and get branches from olive trees, wild olive trees, myrtles, palms, and leafy trees to make temporary shelters, just as it’s written.”

So the people went out, brought back branches, and built shelters for themselves on their rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courtyards of God’s house, and in the squares at the Water Gate and Ephraim’s Gate.
Everyone who’d come back from exile made shelters and lived in them. The Israelites hadn’t done this since the days of Joshua son of Nun. There was so much joy.
Ezra read from the book of God’s law every day, from the first day to the last. They celebrated the festival for seven days and held a solemn gathering on the eighth day, as the law required.
On the twenty-fourth day of that month, the Israelites gathered to fast, dressed in sackcloth and covered with dirt.
The descendants of Israel separated themselves from all foreigners. They stood up and confessed their own sins and the wrongs their ancestors had done.
Standing where they were, they read from the book of the law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day. For another quarter they confessed their sins and worshiped the LORD their God.
The Levites Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani stood on the steps and cried out loudly to the LORD their God.

Then the Levites Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah said, “Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting! May your glorious name be blessed, high above every blessing and every word of praise!

You alone are the LORD. You made the sky, the highest heavens and all their host, the earth and everything on it, the seas and everything in them. You keep them all alive. The host of heaven worships you.
You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees, and named him Abraham.

You found his heart faithful to you and made a covenant to give his descendants the land of the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Jebusite, and Girgashite. You kept your word because you are righteous.
“You saw our ancestors suffering in Egypt and heard them cry out by the Red Sea.

You showed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, his servants, and everyone in his land, because you knew how arrogantly they’d treated our ancestors. You made a name for yourself that lasts to this day.
You split the sea in front of them, and they walked through it on dry ground. You hurled those chasing them into the deep like a stone dropped into raging waters.
You led them by day in a column of cloud and by night in a column of fire, lighting the road they were meant to take.
“You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven. You gave them just rulings, true laws, and good statutes and commands.
You told them about your holy Sabbath and gave them commands, statutes, and a law through your servant Moses.
You gave them bread from heaven when they were hungry and brought water out of the rock when they were thirsty. You told them to go in and take possession of the land you’d sworn to give them.
“But they, our ancestors, got proud and stubborn and wouldn’t listen to your commands.

They refused to obey and forgot the wonders you’d done among them. They dug in their heels and, in their rebellion, picked a leader to take them back into slavery. But you’re a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and full of faithful love. You didn’t abandon them.
They even cast a calf out of metal and said, ‘This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt.’ They said and did things that terribly dishonored you.

Yet in your great mercy, you didn’t abandon them in the wilderness. The column of cloud stayed over them by day to guide them, and the column of fire stayed by night to light the way they were meant to go.
You gave them your good Spirit to teach them. You kept feeding them manna and gave them water when they were thirsty.
“For forty years you kept them going in the wilderness. They lacked nothing. Their clothes didn’t wear out, and their feet didn’t swell.
You gave them kingdoms and peoples and divided them up as their shares. So they took possession of Sihon’s land, the land of the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og, king of Bashan.
You made their children as numerous as the stars in the sky and brought them into the land you’d told their ancestors to go in and take.
“So their children went in and took the land. You subdued the Canaanites who lived there and handed over their kings and the peoples of the land for your people to do with as they saw fit.

They took fortified cities and rich land. They got houses full of good things, wells already dug for storing water, vineyards, olive groves, and loads of fruit trees. They ate their fill, grew fat, and delighted in how good you’d been to them.
“Even so, they disobeyed and rebelled against you. They threw your law behind their backs and killed your prophets who warned them so they’d return to you. They terribly dishonored you.

So you handed them over to their enemies, who made them suffer. When they cried out to you in their trouble, you heard from heaven. In your great mercy you sent people to rescue them from their enemies.

But as soon as they had some peace, they did evil in front of you again. You left them in their enemies’ hands, and those enemies ruled over them. Still, when they came back and cried out to you, you heard from heaven and rescued them over and over in your mercy.

You warned them to bring them back to your law. They got arrogant and ignored your commands. They broke your rulings, the ones a person can live by if they follow them. They turned their backs, got stubborn, and refused to listen.
You put up with them for years. Your Spirit warned them through your prophets, but they wouldn’t listen, so you handed them over to the peoples of the lands.
“Still, in your great mercy, you didn’t wipe them out or abandon them. You’re a gracious and merciful God.

So now, our God, great, mighty, and awesome, you keep your covenant and show faithful love. Please don’t treat as small all the hardship that has fallen on us, our kings, our officials, our priests, our prophets, our ancestors, and all your people from the days of the kings of Assyria right up to today.
You’ve been just in everything that’s happened to us. You’ve acted faithfully, and we’ve done evil.
Our kings, officials, priests, and ancestors didn’t follow your law or listen to your commands or the warnings you gave them.
They didn’t serve you in their own kingdom, even with all the good you gave them and the broad, rich land you set before them. They didn’t turn away from the evil they were doing.
“Look at us now. We’re servants right here in the land you gave our ancestors so they could eat its fruit and enjoy its good things. Here we are, servants in that very land.
The land yields plenty for the kings you’ve set over us because of our sins. They do what they want with our bodies and our livestock. We’re in deep trouble.
Because of all this, we’re making a binding covenant and putting it in writing. Our officials, Levites, and priests are putting their seals on it.”
Here are the people who put their seals on it: Governor Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah,
Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah,
Pashhur, Amariah, Malchijah,
Hattush, Shebaniah, Malluch,
Harim, Meremoth, Obadiah,
Daniel, Ginnethon, Baruch,
Meshullam, Abijah, Mijamin,
Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah. These were the priests.
The Levites were Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui from Henadad’s descendants, and Kadmiel,
along with their fellow Levites Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,
Mica, Rehob, Hashabiah,
Zaccur, Sherebiah, Shebaniah,
Hodiah, Bani, and Beninu.
The people’s leaders were Parosh, Pahathmoab, Elam, Zattu, Bani,
Bunni, Azgad, Bebai,
Adonijah, Bigvai, Adin,
Ater, Hezekiah, Azzur,
Hodiah, Hashum, Bezai,
Hariph, Anathoth, Nobai,
Magpiash, Meshullam, Hezir,
Meshezabel, Zadok, Jaddua,
Pelatiah, Hanan, Anaiah,
Hoshea, Hananiah, Hasshub,
Hallohesh, Pilha, Shobek,
Rehum, Hashabnah, Maaseiah,
Ahiah, Hanan, Anan,
Malluch, Harim, and Baanah.

The rest of the people included the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and everyone who’d separated from the peoples of the lands to follow God’s law. Their wives, sons, and daughters were included too, everyone who could understand what they were agreeing to.

They joined their fellow Israelites, the nobles, and bound themselves with an oath and a curse. They swore to live by God’s law given through Moses, God’s servant, and to follow every command, ruling, and statute of the LORD our Lord.
We agreed that we wouldn’t give our daughters in marriage to the peoples of the land or take their daughters as wives for our sons.

If the peoples of the land bring goods or grain to sell on the Sabbath, we won’t buy from them on the Sabbath or any holy day. We’ll also give up the crops of the seventh year and let every debt go uncollected.
We set a rule for ourselves to give a third of a shekel each year for the service of our God’s house.

That would pay for the bread set out before God, the regular grain and burnt offerings, the Sabbaths, new moons, and appointed festivals, the holy things, the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and all the work of our God’s house.

We, the priests, Levites, and people, drew lots to decide when each family would bring its wood offering to our God’s house. We’d bring it at the appointed times each year to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, just as the law says.
We agreed to bring the first crops from our land and the first fruit from every kind of tree to the LORD’s house every year.
We’d also bring our firstborn sons and livestock, including the firstborn of our herds and flocks, to the priests serving at our God’s house, as the law says.

We’d bring the first of our dough, our wave offerings, fruit from every kind of tree, new wine, and oil to the priests in the storerooms of our God’s house. We’d bring a tenth of what our land produces to the Levites, who collect the tenths in all our farming villages.
A priest descended from Aaron is to be there when the Levites collect the tenths. The Levites are to bring a tenth of what they collect to our God’s house, into the storerooms of the treasury.

The Israelites and Levites are to bring the wave offerings of grain, new wine, and oil to the rooms where the sanctuary vessels are kept and where the serving priests, gatekeepers, and singers are. We won’t neglect our God’s house.
The leaders lived in Jerusalem. Everyone else drew lots so one out of ten would move to Jerusalem, the holy city, and the other nine would live in the other towns.
The people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem.

Here are the leaders of the province who lived in Jerusalem. In Judah’s towns, each lived on their own property: the Israelites, priests, Levites, temple servants, and descendants of Solomon’s servants.
Some people from Judah and Benjamin lived in Jerusalem. From Judah came Athaiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, from the line of Perez.
There was also Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Colhozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite.
Altogether, 468 brave men from the line of Perez lived in Jerusalem.
Here are Benjamin’s descendants: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah.
After him came Gabbai and Sallai. There were 928 in all.
Joel son of Zichri was in charge of them, and Judah son of Hassenuah was second in command over the city.
From the priests there were Jedaiah son of Joiarib, Jachin,
and Seraiah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the official in charge of God’s house.
There were also 822 of their fellow priests who worked at the house, and Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah.
With him were 242 of his relatives who headed their families. There was also Amashsai son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer.
With him were 128 of their fellow priests, brave men. Zabdiel son of Haggedolim was in charge of them.
From the Levites there was Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni.
Shabbethai and Jozabad, two of the Levite leaders, supervised the work outside God’s house.
Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, led off the prayer of thanks. Bakbukiah was second among his fellow Levites. There was also Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun.
There were 284 Levites in the holy city altogether.
The gatekeepers Akkub, Talmon, and their fellow guards kept watch at the gates. There were 172 of them.
The rest of Israel, the priests, and the Levites lived across the towns of Judah, each on their own inherited land.
The temple servants lived on Ophel. Ziha and Gishpa were in charge of them.
Uzzi son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, oversaw the Levites in Jerusalem. He was from the line of Asaph, the singers responsible for the service of God’s house.
The king had issued orders about them, with a regular provision for what the singers needed each day.
Pethahiah son of Meshezabel, from the line of Zerah son of Judah, represented the king in every matter concerning the people.
As for the villages and their fields, some of Judah’s descendants lived in Kiriath Arba and its surrounding towns, Dibon and its towns, and Jekabzeel and its villages.
Others lived in Jeshua, Moladah, and Beth Pelet,
in Hazar Shual, and in Beersheba and its surrounding towns,
in Ziklag, and in Meconah and its towns,
in En Rimmon, Zorah, and Jarmuth,
in Zanoah and Adullam and their villages, in Lachish and its fields, and in Azekah and its towns. They settled from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom.
Benjamin’s descendants lived from Geba onward, in Michmash, Aija, and Bethel and its surrounding towns,
in Anathoth, Nob, and Ananiah,
in Hazor, Ramah, and Gittaim,
in Hadid, Zeboim, and Neballat,
and in Lod and Ono, the Valley of Craftsmen.
Some groups of Levites from Judah settled in Benjamin’s territory.
Here are the priests and Levites who went up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra,
Amariah, Malluch, Hattush,
Shecaniah, Rehum, Meremoth,
Iddo, Ginnethoi, Abijah,
Mijamin, Maadiah, Bilgah,
Shemaiah, Joiarib, Jedaiah,
Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the leaders of the priests and their fellow priests in Jeshua’s time.
The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah. Mattaniah and his fellow Levites led the songs of thanks.
Their fellow Levites Bakbukiah and Unno stood near them at their assigned posts.
Jeshua was Joiakim’s father, Joiakim was Eliashib’s father, and Eliashib was Joiada’s father.
Joiada was Jonathan’s father, and Jonathan was Jaddua’s father.
In Joiakim’s time, these priests headed their families: Meraiah for Seraiah’s family and Hananiah for Jeremiah’s.
Meshullam for Ezra’s family and Jehohanan for Amariah’s.
Jonathan for Malluchi’s family and Joseph for Shebaniah’s.
Adna for Harim’s family and Helkai for Meraioth’s.
Zechariah for Iddo’s family and Meshullam for Ginnethon’s.
Zichri for Abijah’s family. There was also Miniamin’s family, and Piltai was from Moadiah’s.
Shammua for Bilgah’s family and Jehonathan for Shemaiah’s.
Mattenai for Joiarib’s family and Uzzi for Jedaiah’s.
Kallai for Sallai’s family and Eber for Amok’s.
Hashabiah for Hilkiah’s family and Nethanel for Jedaiah’s.
The heads of the Levite families were recorded in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua. The priests were also recorded during the reign of Darius the Persian.
The family heads descended from Levi were recorded in the book of the chronicles through the days of Johanan son of Eliashib.
The Levite leaders were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua son of Kadmiel. Their fellow Levites stood next to them, group by group, to praise and give thanks as David, the man of God, had commanded.
Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were the gatekeepers. They kept watch at the storerooms by the gates.
They served in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua, son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe.

When it was time to dedicate Jerusalem’s wall, they sent for the Levites wherever they lived and brought them to Jerusalem. They celebrated the dedication with joy, giving thanks and singing with cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps.
The singers’ descendants gathered from the plain around Jerusalem and from the Netophathites’ villages.
They came from Beth Gilgal and from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth too. The singers had built villages for themselves around Jerusalem.
The priests and Levites purified themselves. Then they purified the people, the gates, and the wall.
I brought Judah’s leaders up onto the wall and appointed two large groups to give thanks and walk in procession. One group went right along the wall toward the Dung Gate.
Hoshaiah followed them with half of Judah’s leaders.
Azariah, Ezra, and Meshullam went too,
along with Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah.
Some priests’ sons came with trumpets, including Zechariah son of Jonathan, son of Shemaiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Micaiah, son of Zaccur, son of Asaph.
His brothers Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani carried the musical instruments of David, the man of God. Ezra the scribe went ahead of them.
At the Spring Gate they went straight up the stairs of David’s city where the wall rises. They passed above David’s house and went as far as the Water Gate to the east.
The other group giving thanks went the other way to meet them. I followed with half the people on the wall, above the Tower of the Furnaces and as far as the Wide Wall.
They went above Ephraim’s Gate, past the Old Gate and the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of Hammeah, and on to the Sheep Gate. They stopped at the Guard Gate.
So the two groups giving thanks stood in God’s house. I stood there too, with half the officials.
The priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah were there with trumpets,
along with Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. The singers sang out loud under Jezrahiah’s direction.
That day they offered great sacrifices and celebrated because God had filled them with joy. The women and children celebrated too. You could hear Jerusalem’s joy from far away.

That day men were put in charge of the storerooms for the treasures, wave offerings, firstfruits, and tenths. They collected from the fields around the towns the portions the law set aside for the priests and Levites. Judah was glad for the priests and Levites who served.
They carried out their duties to God and their duties of purification. The singers and gatekeepers did likewise, as David and his son Solomon had commanded.
Back in the days of David and Asaph there was a leader of the singers, and there were songs of praise and thanks to God.
In the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel gave the singers and gatekeepers their daily shares. They set aside the Levites’ share, and the Levites set aside the share for Aaron’s descendants.
That day they read aloud to the people from the book of Moses. They found it written there that no Ammonite or Moabite was ever to enter God’s assembly,
because those peoples hadn’t met the Israelites with bread and water. Instead, they hired Balaam to curse them. But our God turned the curse into a blessing.
When they heard what the law said, they separated from Israel the whole mixed group among them.
Before this, Eliashib the priest had been put in charge of the rooms in our God’s house. He was allied with Tobiah,

and had set aside a large room for him. That room had held the grain offerings, frankincense, vessels, the tenths of grain, new wine, and oil assigned to the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the wave offerings for the priests.
I wasn’t in Jerusalem when this happened. In the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, king of Babylon, I’d gone to see the king. After a while I asked his permission to leave.
I returned to Jerusalem and found out what a wrong Eliashib had done for Tobiah by setting up a room for him in the courts of God’s house.
It upset me so much that I threw all of Tobiah’s household belongings out of the room.
Then I ordered them to clean the rooms, and I brought back the vessels from God’s house, along with the grain offerings and frankincense.
I also found out the Levites hadn’t received their shares. The Levites and singers who did the work had all gone back to their fields.
I confronted the officials. “Why has God’s house been neglected?” I gathered the Levites and singers and put them back at their posts.
Then all Judah brought a tenth of the grain, new wine, and oil into the storerooms.

I put Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah the Levite in charge of the storerooms. Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, helped them. They were trusted to hand out the shares to their fellow workers.
Remember me for this, my God. Don’t erase the good I’ve done for your house and its services.

In those days I saw people in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath. They brought in sheaves and loaded donkeys with wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of goods, and carried them into Jerusalem on the Sabbath. I warned them on the day they sold food.
Some people from Tyre lived there too. They brought in fish and all kinds of goods and sold them to the people of Judah in Jerusalem on the Sabbath.
I confronted Judah’s nobles and said, “What is this wrong you’re doing, treating the Sabbath like it isn’t holy?
Didn’t your ancestors do this? Didn’t our God bring all this disaster on us and on this city? Now you’re bringing more anger on Israel by treating the Sabbath like any other day.”

As darkness fell on Jerusalem’s gates before the Sabbath, I ordered the doors shut until the Sabbath was over. I put some of my servants at the gates to keep any loads from being brought in on the Sabbath.
The merchants and sellers of all kinds of goods spent the night outside Jerusalem once or twice.
I warned them, “Why are you staying by the wall? If you do it again, I’ll lay hands on you.” From then on they stopped coming on the Sabbath.
I told the Levites to purify themselves and come guard the gates to keep the Sabbath holy. Remember me for this too, my God, and spare me because your faithful love is so great.
In those days I also saw Jews who’d married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab.
Half their children spoke the language of Ashdod. They couldn’t speak the language of the Jews and spoke the language of their own people instead.

I argued with them, cursed them, struck some of them, and pulled out their hair. I made them swear by God: “Don’t give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters as wives for your sons or yourselves.

Didn’t Solomon king of Israel sin over these things? Among all those nations there was no king like him. His God loved him and made him king over all Israel. Still, even he was led into sin by foreign women.
Are we supposed to listen to you and do this great wrong, sinning against our God by marrying foreign women?”
One of the sons of Joiada son of Eliashib the high priest was Sanballat the Horonite’s son-in-law. So I drove him away from me.
Remember them, my God. They’ve defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priests and Levites.
So I cleared away all foreigners from among them and assigned duties to the priests and Levites, each to their own work,
and arranged for the wood offering at set times and for the firstfruits. Remember me for good, my God.
